summary.text:
Read on the 2026/27 Capital Strategy / TMSS / Prudential Indicators cover paper (49794, Council 19 February 2026, six pages) alongside its Appendix 2 (49796, 20 pages: TMSS body + Appendix A Arlingclose forecast 22 Dec 2025 + Appendix B existing portfolio at 31 Dec 2025). The cover paper is a framework document; every substantive figure sits in Appendix 2. The 2025/26 mid-year cover paper (49754, same agenda) is a two-page pointer whose Appendix A (49755) was not opened — the 31/12/2025 balance is already carried in the strategy paper's Appendix B and no additional facts are cited from the mid-year here. Appendix 4 (49798) not opened; the treasury story is complete on the two papers read.

Balance sheet identity ties across the four-year window on the loans side (PFI/leases sit separately, per §4.3 and the Table 2 heading 'Loans CFR'): 83.2 - 53.8 = 29.4 at 31.3.26, and the same subtraction ties exactly at 31.3.27, 31.3.28 and 31.3.29. Liability benchmark arithmetic reproduces to the £0.1m rounding on the £11.1/£11.2 first row and exactly thereafter.

The distinctive thing about this paper is the shape between Table 1 and Table 2. The liability benchmark — the paper's own minimum-risk level of external borrowing — sits at £21.2m to £26.4m across the four years. Committed external borrowing sits at £53.8m falling to £51.3m. So the Council carries around £33m of external borrowing today above the benchmark, narrowing to £25m by 2029, offset by treasury investments of £42.6m falling to £34.9m. That gap is not created by choice — it is the shape the 2012 HRA settlement left in place: 53% of the borrowing sits in the 10-20 year maturity bucket (§6.6), i.e. loans maturing in the late 2030s and early 2040s, and can't be repaid without going through the PWLB premature repayment formula. Which is exactly what §4.14 gestures at: 'the recent rise in interest rates means that more favourable debt rescheduling opportunities should arise than in previous years.' On today's DMO curve those long-dated low-coupon loans sit at deep discounts (our engine prices a c.£8m net discount across the seven live loans we hold at c.£49.85m — indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and no MRP or accounting treatment modelled).

The email leads on the Table 1 / Table 2 shape, adds §4.14 with the loan-analysis page as the natural companion, and closes with a small cross-check where their own 5.30% new-long-term-loan assumption at §2.13 aligns with the 10y PWLB Certainty rate implied by their own Arlingclose Appendix A (4.52% 10y gilt + 0.80% Certainty add-on = 5.32%). No loan-book aggregate figure is quoted in the email: the price_book --as-at 2025-12-31 query returned only 1 loan of £1.75m against their published £50.56m PWLB, a false-low result from the Start-field artefact flagged in EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md. The current-position profile in the same tool does hold 7 loans totalling £49.85m, which ties within £0.7m of their 31/12/2025 aggregate on plausible EIP amortisation — so the book is essentially correctly held, but per PIPELINE.md the aggregate stays out of the draft where the year-end reconciliation formally failed.

Officer contact: Anna Crouch, Head of Finance, anna.crouch@nwleicestershire.gov.uk, named on the cover paper 49794 p.6 (and again on the mid-year cover 49754 p.2 with the same address). Meeting date 19 February 2026 is six months past; send window is open to next quarterly Audit and Governance treasury monitoring, date not published.

officer.body:
Hi Anna,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the strategy paper that went to Council on 19 February, ahead of the next quarterly treasury update at Audit and Governance. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is clearly laid out and the balance sheet and liability benchmark tables foot to the pound, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

What drew us in was reading your Table 2 against your Table 1. Your liability benchmark sits at £21.2m in March 2026 rising to £26.4m by March 2029 — the minimum-risk external position after balance-sheet resources are drawn down to a £10m liquidity floor. Your committed external borrowing is £53.8m today, running off to £51.3m across the same window. So about £33m of external borrowing sits above the benchmark today, narrowing to £25m by 2029, offset by treasury investments of £42.6m falling to £34.9m. Of the district books we've read this year, most show the opposite shape — external well below CFR, with internal borrowing doing most of the work — because reserves are thinner. Yours is largely the shape the 2012 HRA settlement left in place: 53% of your borrowing sits in the 10-20 year bucket at §6.6, maturing in the late 2030s and early 2040s.

Which is what makes your paragraph 4.14 timely. You write there that 'the recent rise in interest rates means that more favourable debt rescheduling opportunities should arise than in previous years.' On today's PWLB premature repayment curve, the long-dated, low-coupon HRA loans that dominate the book sit at discounts to par. The per-loan indicative valuation against DMO notice 314/26 is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, priced each day. It is indicative only — only the DMO can quote a real settlement, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment — so nothing follows from it as advice. The direction it shows sits in the same one your own paragraph does.

One small cross-check on the assumption side. Your §2.13 puts new long-term borrowing at 5.30% for the budget. On the Arlingclose curve you print at Appendix A, that lands within a couple of basis points of today's 10-year PWLB Certainty rate (4.52% 10y gilt + 0.80% add-on = 5.32%), and just below the very long-end HRA rate (5.16% + 0.40% = 5.56%). Not a comment on the choice — only where it sits on the curve your own paper carries.

CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put the liability benchmark in front of every finance committee. Yours is already there. The interactive version on our site plots the same curves against real-time PWLB and internal-borrowing paths, and may be useful as a member-facing reference the next time the strategy comes round.

The pages you'll get most from are pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis for the rescheduling arithmetic, and pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity for how the sector is drawing right now — split by HRA and General Fund, by tenor and by council.

On training, three fit: Reading the PWLBpredict and SONIA Forward Curve & OIS sit close to §§2.10 and 2.13, and The Premature Repayment Curve is the natural companion to §4.14. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find any of it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. Word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy and Prudential Indicators 2026/27 — Council 19 February 2026, with Appendix 2 (TMSS 2026/27), its Appendix A (Arlingclose Economic & Interest Rate Forecast, 22 December 2025) and Appendix B (Existing Investment & Debt Portfolio Position, 31 December 2025).
